subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PROTECTION FOR SUBSCRIBERS AGAINST FURTHER RATE INCREASES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. Since senior Bell Canada executives have stated that that company intends to approach the CRTC before this year's end for another rate increase, and whereas a June 1, 1977 rate decision increased company revenue by $162 million and a January 1976 rate decision increased Bell's coffers by $110.3 million, and in light of the fact that Bell executives cite delays due to public hearings in receiving approval of the $162 million increase as a justification for the new application, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan):
That this House instruct the CRTC to protect telephone subscribers from further uncalled for rate increases by reassessing Bell's profitability by examining the earnings of Bell's subsidiaries, and further that the CRTC not speed up public hearings to suit the corporate interests of Bell over those of its subscribers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that the government of Quebec has now presented Bill 101 and that that bill has no changes in the provisions restricting the right to English language education of Canadian children moving from other provinces, I wonder if the Prime Minister will tell the House whether he or the constitutional advisers to the government have this matter under consideration? What options are they considering now in light of the fact that this bill is almost certain to be passed by the Parti Quebecois majority in the Quebec legislature?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were certainly surprised and saddened to see that the bill was brought back under a new number without any change in this very fundamental provision, to which the federal government has indicated its opposition. It is still a formal bill and it will be heard by the relevant committee of the Quebec legislature. We are still hopeful that the Parti Quebecois government will see its way clear to change this very serious infraction of the right of Canadians to move across the country. In its present form, it looks as if the Parti Quebecois is acting as
July 14, 1977

though the province were already separated. This is a point of view we most seriously deny and attack.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: The federal government's position on this has been made very clear, to wit that English-speaking Canadians from other parts of Canada should be able to move into Quebec and have their children go to the official language school of their choice when such schools exist and are justified by numbers of English-speaking Canadians.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: And vice veisa.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Yes, we have also indicated in our policy that, vice versa, French-speaking Canadians moving from Quebec to other centres where there are sufficient numbers of Frenchspeaking Canadians should find schools in that language so that they can exercise the same freedom to move and have their children educated in the language of their choice.
The Leader of the Opposition asks if there has been a reference to the Department of Justice. Certainly, the minister and I have discussed this matter, but there would not be a formal reference of a bill to his law officers until that bill became law and until the constitutionality or otherwise of the bill was made an object of study by the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Just so we are clear, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has repeated the principle that he says guides the attitude of his government. He indicated that the only action the government has taken to this point is that there has been a discussion between himself and the Minister of Justice. There has been no reference to the law officers of the Crown to get a legal opinion of the constitutionality of a bill that holds every likelihood of being passed into law by the government of Quebec. Does the Prime Minister agree that citizens who are facing passage of a law which calls into question long standing rights that they have exercised are entitled to some reassurance from the government of Canada that this government will concern itself with their problems. What kind of reassurance is the Prime Minister prepared to give those Canadians today?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: BILINGUALISM
subsubtopic: RESTRICTION OF RIGHT TO ENGLISH LANGUAGE EDUCATION UNDER QUEBEC'S BILL 101-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I dealt with this matter a few weeks ago when the Secretary of State tabled his paper on language policy. 1 indicated it was our hope that the provinces within the area of education, an area in their constitutional jurisdiction, would want to protect the linguistic rights of the official minorities in their provinces. I went further and said we would be prepared to envisage a constitutional amendment which would give the federal government the authority in the area of education to step in and protect those rights.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM

We are still hopeful that Bill 101 will be amended. If it is not and it passes into law, we will pursue the two courses that I just indicated, get the provinces together to try to obtain from them some guar-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REFERRING QUEBEC'S BILL 101 TO SUPREME COURT
speechtext: Of course, we would keep open the possibility of intervening in a court case as, incidentally, we have done in Manitoba in a case which is not completely dissimilar, at least in so far as language rights are concerned. Here again, it would depend on our views on the constitutionality or otherwise of that particular piece of legislation. I should tell the Leader of the Opposition that in matters of education, I, personally, am not speaking yet as one who has been advised by the Minister of Justice or that department but I, personally, have always taken the view that educational rights were for the province to legislate upon and that there were only certain confessional aspects of those rights which permitted the federal government to intervene and plead ultra vires in that particular decision. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REFERRING QUEBEC'S BILL 101 TO SUPREME COURT

subtopic: POSSIBILITY OF REFERRING QUEBEC'S BILL 101 TO SUPREME COURT

RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext: I am sure we all share the hope of the Prime Minister that the law now before the Quebec National Assembly will be more to our taste and more in accordance with our views than at present. I now seek some elucidation from the Prime Minister. Is he not using the word "right" in two senses? His government has stated most categorically that, subject to circumstances which may make a deferment of application necessity, Canadians have a right to have their children educated in the official language of their choice. Now, he has just said that the right within the field is in the provincial jurisdiction. Is the government of Canada in fact declaring that Canadians do have this right, or is it more accurate to state that they express the hope that this right will be appealed some day?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Halifax knows the answer to that question, but I would certainly repeat it for him. In areas of provincial jurisdiction we can express hopes that rights will be respected, but we cannot legislate in those areas. Naturally, the paper tabled by the Secretary of State a couple of weeks ago covered the whole area of languages in Canada. Some matters can be legislated exclusively by the provinces. Because of that, how-

ever, we did not feel that we should be precluded from expressing the view that we have of Canadian citizens and how this country should be operated as one country. It is in that sense that we talked of rights; not in the legal sense, but as they should be.

subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, whatever differences we may have in some areas I do not think there are any differences between myself and the right hon. gentleman on the subject of languages. Having said that, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether it is appropriate for the federal government to declare rights or to appear to declare rights in areas of provincial jurisdiction, and whether it is really in the interests of national unity for the federal government to appear to declare a right for Canadian citizens and have that challenged by a province within a matter of weeks. I ask that question most earnestly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext: I suppose this is a question of approach and of tactics. The hon. gentleman indicates that we are probably agreed on substance in so far as our belief in language policy. However, in so far as this particular question is concerned, we, in our paper tabled by the Secretary of State, did not hesitate to use the word "right" because we intended to signal to the provinces that we think this particular right should exist in the constitution.

subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will recall that in 1971 at Victoria we indeed stated rights that did not exist, relative to entrenching the official languages in the constitution. They were not rights in the sense that they did not then exist in the constitutional sense, but we wanted them to become constitutional rights. We are saying the same thing in this particular area about the right of minorities in Canada to be able to move where they want in Canada and to be able to continue having their children educated in the official language of their choice.

subtopic: RIGHT TO EDUCATION IN OFFICIAL LANGUAGE OF CHOICE-GOVERNMENT'S INTERPRETATION OF "RIGHT"

NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Last week the National Energy Board indicated to the petroleum industry its willingness to consider applications to increase gas exports to the United States during the next five to seven years. As a result two companies, TransCanada Pipeline and Pan-Alberta Gas, are now stepping up their purchase contracts to a combined total of 1.5 billion cubic feet per day, and they claim that they do not anticipate any difficulties or delays in getting National Energy Board approval to export part of this gas.
In view of the fact that the last report of the National Energy Board foresees a shortage of gas in Canada at the earliest by 1982 and at the latest by 1985, does the government approve of stepping up gas exports to the United States in view of the pessimistic and gloomy forecast which the National Energy Board has made with respect to Canada's anticipated gas shortages within the next five to eight years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government has not been asked to approve and we have not been given any reasons why we should approve.

subtopic: NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am raising the question with the minister because I thought he would be aware of the action of the National Energy Board and would be willing to give the government's views to the National Energy Board if not to the House. In the proposal being made it is now suggested that the increased exports to the United States should be on a swap arrangement by which Alberta gas would be sold in exchange for Alaskan gas to be delivered when the pipeline is built.
Does the minister not think that this means Canada will be selling cheap gas to our American neighbours and in due course purchasing Alaskan gas at two or three times the price we have received for the Alberta gas? I should like to ask the minister if he considers this to be in the best interests of Canadian consumers and whether he proposes to make any representations to the National Energy Board who, after all, are appointed to protect the interests of Canadian consumers?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand very well the question the hon. member is raising about selling now and buying back later on a more expensive basis. The National Energy Board raised this sort of question in its recent report with respect to the Arctic gas pipeline questions. Those are the sorts of questions which members in the coming weeks during the debate in the House of Commons, will have an opportunity to examine. Undoubtedly, there will be considerations which will bear upon the final decision of the government.
Oral Questions

subtopic: NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The National Energy Board report speaks of the gas surplus "bubble" and points out quite properly that many of the gas companies want to sell their gas. If they cannot sell it in Canada they want to sell it in the United States in order to get sufficient financing for further exploration. That is understandable. I want to ask the minister if he or the government as a whole have given any consideration to the advisability of using Petro-Canada to buy gas in the ground, as is done in many countries and as has been done in Saskatchewan for many years where they bought gas in the ground in Saskatchewan and in Alberta as well. Such a procedure would enable the companies to get the necessary cash flow to continue exploration programs while at the same time retaining the cheap gas for the future needs of Canadians rather than swapping it now and having to pay very high prices to get Alaskan gas years later?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATURAL GAS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: In general terms, Mr. Speaker, I have had discussions with senior officers of Petro-Canada about the gas situation in Alberta and what part of Petro-Canada might play with respect to the development of those resources. As the hon. member knows, those resources are subject to the controls and regulations of the Alberta government. I think one of the ways of alleviating the situation with the gas producers who have found gas, as the hon. member pointed out, largely as a result of the incentives which the Alberta government and this government have provided through higher prices-something which he has resisted-might be the pro-rationing by the Alberta government.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I called it six o'clock last night 1 had begun to tell the House of my experience in committee regarding this particular bill which was discussed at length and in great detail. I told my colleagues of the frustrations I suffered, as a layman, being exposed to the intricacies of committee and the House of Commons. I also mentioned my shock and dismay at the interventions by groups of individuals throughout the country who came before the committee. These groups consisted of people from law societies, civil liberties associations and persons who indulged in hunting and trap shooting. All these people felt their individual rights and freedoms were being threatened.
When closure was imposed in committee it was decided that no further witnesses should be heard on this bill. It was my understanding that there were 24 applications from people who wished to have their views and concerns considered by this committee. As I said last night, I cannot understand the indecent haste which has been attached to these measures. The measures are not designed to address themselves to the critical need which exists in our society today-a need to confront organized crime. The minister hangs his hat on gun control and electronic surveillance. These measures are designed to combat organized crime which is now rampant in our country, according to the minister. We do not see any meaningful tool or purpose in Bill C-51 which addresses itself to this critical situation.
We hear much about freedom of information these days. Some of my colleagues on this side of the House, and particularly the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), have almost exclusively concerned themselves for the last two or three years with the matter of freedom of information and openness by the government. Yet the government seems to be going the other way and feels that freedom of information will be achieved by wiretapping persons' phones. We have to ask ourselves for whom is this freedom of information laid before us in the green paper. Will the Liberal government have access to all information exchanged in this country?
As they retract into their shells and tighten up the leaks which trickle away from the ivory towers this government is operating out of these days, they want everyone else in our society to surrender some of the personal freedoms they have enjoyed. These are to be surrendered to the guardians whom

they espouse to be guardians of civil rights and liberties which are to be turned over for the good of the country.
The House of Commons is representative of the people themselves. We are supposed to deal in blind trust. We are supposed to be blindly trusting of this government in their transactions, be they in business or in public spirit. All one needs to do to become a senior official of the government today is to place his holdings in blind trust. But no one ever defines what the phrase "blind trust" means. The government wants us to blindly trust them because they are all good, divine, the seraphs of this world, the angels with seven wings. They can do no evil; they can do no wrong. Recently we have learned that there are, even in that supreme group on the other side, some rotten apples.
I wonder whether the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has looked seriously at all the implications of this bill before us, particularly in the area of electronic eavesdropping. As the minister has indicated, there was no law in existence before 1973 to protect us against a police officer entering our homes and placing bugs on our telephones. The police officer was prohibited from searching our homes or removing any files or property; but he could enter our residences and put electronic devices in place in order to monitor conversations. There was no law against that practice in 1973 or 1974, and thus we addressed ourselves to it. Yet we are about to pass a law now making it legal. I wonder if the minister has really thought that out. If it was legal to do such a thing at that time, can you imagine some police officer abusing his power and breaking into 24 Sussex Drive when guests are staying there who are student radicals and campus revolutionaries?
Can you imagine the telephone at 24 Sussex Drive being bugged and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) receiving a telephone call from Bill Teron, who is the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the following conversation occurring, "Mr. Prime Minister, I think you should have a swimming pool. As you know, my public companies are in blind trust and I cannot talk about them. Some of my cement trucks will be running around the city and they would not mind dropping off a few loads there. I do not want you to know where the cement or the money is coming from. What do you think?" Imagine Keith Davey telephoning the Prime Minister and saying, "What do you think about calling an election? As you are aware, I am a shareholder of a little company that grows flowers. Since you wear a flower in the House of Commons, how about a contract?"
We are all human. The Prime Minister is human, Keith Davey is human, Bill Teron is human, and so is any police officer. Just because a police officer has yellow stripes on his pants does not indicate he is different. He is a human being. This blind trust is going to be abused, because human nature applies equally to everyone. It applies equally to me, to my colleagues on this side of the House and to my friends on the other side of the House. I wonder whether the minister has taken all these things into consideration.
Let me tell you about some of the things said in committee. One day several representatives of the Law Society of Upper
July 14, 1977

Canada appeared before the committee. These representatives were lawyers who established the terms of reference and the code of ethics for all benchers of the Upper Canada region, which is Ontario. They were telling us that most of the criminal lawyers who operate in the city of Toronto will no longer speak to their clients over the telephone. All too often, at great expense, a senior law counsel advises his client to meet him somewhere in the dark on a park bench. He must ask him to go to the additional expense of hiring a taxi in order to meet in a park, because he can no longer trust the telephone. This should concern all members. It concerns me and all Canadians that we are surrendering rights and privileges enshrined in the Bill of Rights and every other piece of law and human justice that we have ever conceived.
How far can we go in trusting this government with the rights and freedoms that we once enjoyed? Does anyone think that organized crime will worry about this wiretap law? Is anyone so naive as to think they will use the telephone when plotting their sinister schemes? Of course not. They have worked out codes. They have worked out their own delivery systems. They could not trust the mail 20 years ago, and now they cannot trust the telephone. They know how to react.
The innocent, unsuspecting, law-abiding citizen does not have the money or the technology to react to this law. His telephone will be tapped. As the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) stated, he may want to call his doctor, who may be one of ten doctors in the clinic along with 30 nurses and five or six secretaries. One of them might be suspected of having committed a criminal act. The telephone conversations of everyone in the clinic will be tapped and be placed on the computer somewhere. Telephone companies are now producing new systems, having discovered that a person's voice is as clear an identification as his thumbprint or fingerprint. One person in 20 million can be identified over the telephone by closing the gap on the sound waves over the telephone system by computer. At this time we should be protecting ourselves, passing legislation against that kind of gadgetry which could abuse the rights of individuals. Instead, we are making all this information more accessible to the police.
The hon. member for Calgary North said there is no longer any need to do police work or operate a police academy; all you have to do is run the Bell Telephone system through the police station, have an army of people there to identify every individual who uses the telephone, and put their voices and comments in the computer. You need only push a button to get the conversation, and any judge will act accordingly. This is very frightening. Thousands of Canadians are writing to their members of parliament. Letters are pouring into our offices, as I am sure they are into the offices of the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). I have here two letters which I will read. They are short. I chose them for that reason. The first was sent to the chairman of the committee. I quote;
Criminal Code
Bill C-51 is developing within me, as a Canadian citizen, an inferiority complex due to the fact that our elected members of government fail to realize that such a bill is eroding away my freedom as a Canadian.
I cannot help but ask that the complete firearms section of Bill C-51 be banished once and for all.
There are other such pieces of legislation. This kind of action is not restricted to the bills of the Minister of Justice. Other bills give this government powers beyond anything that any government in any free society has, particularly a government that works under a parliamentary system such as ours. Last week we dealt with Bill C-38. One of my constituents wrote to me as follows:
I would like to express my grave concern regarding the proposed Bill C-38 amending the Fisheries Act. The terms of the bill are so sweeping, the definitions so broad, that anyone near or on any body of water could be deemed in violation of the act in some way. This coupled with the draconian penalties provided by the proposed amendments to the Criminal Code place very broad discretionary powers in the hands of enforcement agencies. There would appear to be little regard for the scale of damage or the cost-benefit relationships of any project that may impinge even marginally on waterways.
The search without warrant powers granted to inspectors under section 9 would seem to be an obvious infringement of basic civil liberties.
My constituent obviously does not know what has happened in the past few years-in this government's term of office. The just society, human liberties and human justice have become a myth. They are something we once knew. We expected our government to keep them in sacred trust for us. As the hon. member for Calgary North said yesterday, and as the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, the "just society" is just for the Liberal government but not for anyone else. The hangers on are also part of the just society, the sick minds sitting on the other side of the House which have conceived and perpetrated this legislation on us.
There is no way this bill can pass this House. We cannot condone this kind of action going unchecked. We do not have to subject ourselves to this kind of intimidation. Incidentally, intimidation is one thing for which a judge can allow a wiretap to be placed on someone's telephone. I would like a wiretap placed on the telephone of the Minister of Justice, because he intimidated members on this side of the House when he appeared on the scene of an unfortunate incident.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order. I do not want the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) deliberately to mislead the House and insult me by saying that I am one of the legal profession. I participated in this debate as a layman, and I am proud of it.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Order, please. I suggest to the hon. member that is not a point of order, but a point of debate.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point of order is well taken. I did not intend to label anyone in this House as a lawyer. I thought I might put before the House some ideas with regard to this bill. I am caught on the horns of a dilemma with regard to Bill C-51. The bill includes gun control legislation, wiretap legislation and some parole provisions. 1 am trying to protect not only the particular concerns of my constituents but the concerns and the welfare of all Canadians, and I find myself in some difficulty because in principle I believe there should be some control and proper processing of those who intend to obtain firearms and to use them. I feel that the time has come in Canada to move in that direction.

Accompanying Bill C-51 are the wiretap provisions. I find myself in some quandary with respect to those provisions because, on the one hand, I recognize the need of my fellow Canadians for security which can be met by controlling the acquisition of firearms and, on the other hand, I am stuck with the problem of being asked to support some provisions in Bill C-51 to provide law enforcement agencies in the country with the power to wiretap. That is the dilemma in which I find myself as a member of parliament. I would like to raise some questions. I suppose the government felt this was a pretty cute way of putting things together in one bill, which might be called an omnibus bill, and in this way to get a bill which had certain provisions which appealed to the majority of members of parliament, but also some distasteful aspects of the legislation, passed by the House.
We also have a problem in terms of the Canadian people's perception of the security of the state. Most people who have written to me about Bill C-51 have written about the gun control section. Very few people have turned their attention to the wiretap provisions. I recognize the fact that probably those who were writing on the gun control provisions are a well organized group. It is a lobby operating with the aim of persuading and convincing members of parliament that they should not pass that section of Bill C-51. But those people
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
forget about the other part of the bill, namely, the wiretap provisions.
In discussions of this matter with my constituents and other people, the response I usually get is that, after all, they do not care if the police listen to their conversations, because they are not doing anything wrong. That sort of thinking pervades the minds of Canadians. They think that in fact we should give that right to law enforcement officers and agencies to ensure the maintenance of our security and freedom. I consider this to be a very serious step. What we on this side of the House have been trying to put across to the government is that when you extend wiretapping provisions, which is what this clause in the bill will do, when you extend occasions for wiretapping and you extend the notification period, it is an extremely important step.
At present, wiretapping is permitted for the smallest of crimes, such as even the smuggling of a pair of shorts across the border. It seems to me that wiretapping should not even be contemplated, and certainly such a decision should not be made at the snap of one's fingers, because wiretapping invades the privacy not only of the individual concerned but also of the person who is contacting him. Privacy is one of the rights to which Canadians are entitled, and that right should be protected. Much is made of the right to privacy between client and lawyer, patient and doctor, and confessor and sinner. That right is greatly respected.
However, there is also the right to privacy between citizens. They should have the right to hold private conversations. When we decide to broaden the wiretapping provisions, we decide to take an extremely serious step. I think that if I were to weigh the seriousness of widening the accessibility to wiretapping by law enforcement officers and agencies against the existence of crime, I would be prepared to protect the right to privacy and recognize that there is crime in the community and that we have to find a more effective method of dealing with it. So if I had to make that trade-off, I would say there should be no wiretapping at all, for anyone-private citizen, agency, or law enforcement officer.
The question that comes to my mind is whether accessibility to wiretapping makes a law enforcement agency more effective. Would the widening of this provision make that agency more efficient? I have grave doubts about it. I argue that all it does is to encourage laziness and slothfulness. To get an order permitting wiretapping is the easy way to go about it. We can keep a 24-hour tap on somebody's phone and listen to thousands and thousands of conversations-goodness knows for how long. Is it more efficient and productive to have three-man shifts listening in on a wiretap, or is it more efficient to infiltrate organized crime and obtain evidence in this more direct way? Will it not make a law enforcement agency more efficient to develop good detective techniques, thus encouraging excellence in detective work which is so essential in ensuring that crime is eliminated in a community?
The question that occurs to me, as well, is this: What has been the experience, in terms of the conviction rate, with the use of wiretaps? Can the minister tell the House whether, in
July 14, 1977

countries which have permitted wiretapping, the conviction rate has been studied in terms of a cost-benefit analysis? Has this been a more effective means of bringing lawbreakers to heel? Has there been a higher conviction rate, and can the minister provide us with any experiences proving that?
I am prepared to listen. As the hon. member for New Westminister (Mr. Leggatt) has pointed out, we had Ramsey Clark, former attorney general of the U.S., before the committee. Mr. Clark pointed out that wiretapping is the most inefficient method of busting criminals. The minister argued that wiretapping would help us get at dons in the mafia. Surely the mafia does not use telephones to set up contracts. The technique is to go beyond the borders of countries where there is wiretapping. The mafia holds conferences where there is no wiretapping and where there are weak police forces. Is the minister prepared to tell me that where wiretapping is in effect the conviction rate is higher? Can he give me examples? If he can, I am certainly prepared to listen to his argument.
Citizens have the right to privacy. The statement made in many letters I have received with regard to the gun control part of Bill C-51 is that people have the right to bear firearms and that the gun control part of this bill is contrary to their rights. It seems to me that the right to privacy has been completely forgotten. The government seems to be playing on the fears of the Canadian people. It seems to imply that organized crime is taking over and that people ought to trade off their right to privacy so that the law enforcement forces can invade that privacy.
The hon. member for New Westminster has taken a strong position on the question of wiretapping. It has been pointed out that we do not need this, and that there are more effective ways of putting a stop to criminal activities. The hon. member's amendment suggests that if we are going to use wiretapping, it ought to be used in relation to very serious crimes which would be punishable on conviction by ten years' imprisonment or more. The hon. member tried to delineate that in his amendment.
I cannot impress enough upon hon. members the seriousness of extending wiretapping. The telephones of members of this House have been tapped. If this bill goes through as proposed by the government, members of parliament might never know about these things because three years down the line many of us will no longer be members of parliament. We might never find out that conversations between ourselves and our constituents which we thought were private were not private at all. I call on hon. members to consider these important matters, and perhaps the minister should answer some questions. Can he assure the House that wiretapping increases the rate of convictions? What is the rate in jurisdictions which have used wiretapping?
Can the minister show us that the use of wiretapping has made law enforcement agencies more effective? Is there a risk of taking away the privacy of individuals? Will wiretapping invade privacy? How does that stand up against the right to
Criminal Code

I am also rising because I listened with dismay to the speech made yesterday afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford). I have always considered the Minister of Justice a very reasonable person. I have had considerable respect for his ability both as a lawyer and as a parliamentarian, but I could not help but feel yesterday that he put up a most unfair defence of a very weak piece of legislation in regard to dealing with electronic surveillance.
The minister began by setting forth the terms of the legislation which was passed in 1974. That was good legislation. It should be remembered that in 1974 we had a minority government and therefore the government was compelled to get the co-operation of the opposition groups. That legislation on the statute books was designed to stop private wiretapping and eavesdropping; to provide for police electronic surveillance under clearly stipulated conditions; and to provide that persons whose telephones were tapped were to be given notice in due course that their telephone conversations were tapped.
Yesterday the minister told the House that this legislation has not worked. He did not tell us why it has not worked. He said that it is difficult for a judge to define what is meant by "organized crime". Very well, Mr. Speaker, if that is true, the minister should have brought in some legislation more clearly defining what is meant by "organized crime". But how does allowing wiretapping to be used in evidence in court, and extending the time for reporting to those people who have been spied upon to three years, clarify what is organized crime? The minister has a responsibility to tell the House why the present

In quoting the police and the attorneys general of the provinces, the minister is implying that the judges have been uncooperative in giving authorization. Is that true? Is the minister saying that the police had difficulty getting authorization from judges? It would be a terrible indictment of the judiciary of this country. If the police have been getting co-operation, then why does the minister now need provisions allowing the tapes which are taken of a wiretap to be used in court as evidence?
The minister stated the basic principles here. First of all, he said, we are all opposed to private wiretapping. Agreed. He said we are also agreed that the police should be allowed to indulge in electronic surveillance under what he calls "proper judicial supervision". I, for one, Mr. Speaker, do approve. 1 think there are times when it may be that wiretapping and other forms of electronic surveillance are necessary in order to deal with criminals and to stop criminal activities in this country. That is why we voted for the legislation of 1974. But we voted for it on the understanding that these wiretapping operations would only be permitted when authorization had been granted by the courts.
The minister is now saying that he wants electronic surveillance under, to quote his words, "proper judicial supervision". How can there be proper judicial supervision when the police can wiretap and eavesdrop, and then take the tapes into court and have them accepted as evidence? Why would the police bother to go to court to get permission, if they can use the evidence in court? The simplest thing to do is to go on a witch-hunt, a fishing expedition, wire enough people and tap enough phones so that if nothing of interest is found except some petty gossip they do not need to do anything with it. That is, except to keep it on the record because it might be useful on a further occasion for a little blackmail. However, if the police do find something, Mr. Speaker, which they got illegally, by breaking the law, then they can take it into court and use it as evidence against a person who is charged.
Just where are we going, Mr. Speaker? What the minister is saying is that when you ask the question, "What is a crime?", the answer is that a crime is an illegal act which is committed by the police. If the police break the law, or if they tap phones by using eavesdropping facilities illegally, that is not a crime; the reward is that the evidence can be used in court in order to convict some individual.
I wonder whether the minister and the House realize the road down which we are travelling. At the present time, as I understand the law, the police cannot break into my house or office, or any other person's premises, in order to secure documents unless they first obtain a search warrant or writ of assistance. Is the next step going to be that they can break in illegally? There is some evidence that the police have broken in illegally, which is why the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) has ordered an investigation into the RCMP. But if they break into premises illegally, are they to be allowed to use any

documents which they find as evidence, in court? That will be the next step.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: The minister's interjection seems to me to point not down the road which we might travel, but down the road which we are already travelling. Surely what happened in the United States is a lesson to this country. The CIA set up its "dirty tricks" department where the "plumbers" were illegally breaking into premises, not to deal with criminals but to get political information against their political opponents. That has built up to the point where we know Edgar Hoover got private dossiers on people in public life, such as senators, congressmen and people like Martin Luther King. Is that what we want to do? There is now evidence that the CIA had assassination squads in South Vietnam. Why? On the assumption that the forces who are supposed to maintain the law can violate the law any time they pleased, it is in the interests of national security to do so. If we start down that road, we are going to find ourselves in exactly the same kind of difficulty from which the United States is now emerging.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Surely, in this country, if an act is illegal for ordinary citizens it is illegal for the police.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE

Louis XIV once said, "L'etat c'est moi"-which means, "I am the state". In a democracy, this government is not the state; it is the servant of the state.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I will deal with motion No. 30 amending clause 9 at page 49 by striking out lines 23 to 31 and substituting the words "consultation with clients". The clause reads:
No authorization may be given to intercept a private communication at the office of residence of a solicitor, or at any other place ordinarily used by a solicitor and by other solicitors for the purpose of consultation with clients,
If the clause stopped at this point, that would be fine, but it goes on to read:
-unless the judge to whom the application is made is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the solicitor, any other solicitor practising with him, any person employed by him or any other such solicitor or a member of the solicitor's household has been or is about to become a party to an offence.
The first point I want to make is that all communications between clients and solicitor should be privileged and confidential. Otherwise, no solicitor could act for his client or use the telephone in privacy. There have been cases of telephones in courthouses being wiretapped and there have also been cases of phones in law offices being wiretapped. This means that if the police suspect one person in that office of, say, smoking marijuana or doing something within the definition of offence in the amendment moved by my good friend, and there are 100 lawyers in that law firm, 30 or 40 secretaries and several
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
bookeepers, they can wiretap the whole office so that all the private conversations can be listened to in the hope that they can hear one sentence which would help them obtain evidence against the one person they suspect.
Let us consider a medical clinic with 20 or 30 doctors practising together, specialists in different fields. If the police were to suspect a clerk, an orderly, a nurse or even a doctor in that office, all the conversations could be tapped for 60 long days, all the most private matters that were discussed concerning our wives, our children and ourselves and concerning all other Canadians, could be overheard. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) said in his brilliant speech this afternoon, this could happen. But he could have added one sentence-namely, that this information could have been fed into a computer.
There are unfortunate cases of high school girls 14 or 15 years old becoming pregnant, calling the family doctor and telling him of their misfortune. If that clinic were wiretapped, the record of that girl's conversation could be overheard and fed into the computer. If my unmarried daughter should become pregnant, or if that were to happen to anyone else, I would not want that published in the Calgary Herald or the Toronto Star. I see a few doctors present in the House. They know how private some medical information can be, and that the privilege of confidentiality is not to protect lawyers or doctors but to protect clients and patients.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) spoke about exemptions, but there is no exemption here. It says that no authorization will be given unless the judge to whom the application is made is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for it. Anyone can be suspected in a solicitor's office, his partner, someone working for him, someone on his staff at home, such as the gardener, the maid or the fellow who sands the floors.
As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands pointed out, the police cannot enter your home without a search warrant or a writ of assistance, but they can smuggle in by wiretapping a telephone, by putting a bug in your front room, or even under your bed. This is what this amendment is all about. As the right hon. member for Prince Albert said this afternoon, surely the minister will show some sanity in reference to this matter. This is a reasonable amendment. I will quote from the brief in a few moments. The minister read from the brief and he said that the Advocates' Society of Ontario did not agree with my good friend, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). 1 question the fact that is an accurate statement, but even if it is an accurate statement, the Advocates' Society came before the committee on June 9 with three very intelligent legal briefs. In one of them they said:
The present sections of the Criminal Code make no special provision for the interception of communications to and by solicitors. If there are reasonable grounds for belief that a solicitor is a person the interception of whose private communications may assist the investigation of an offence, an authorization will be granted to intercept his communications.
This is at the discretion of the judge. The minister says he trusts judges. I have a lot of respect for our judiciary, but this is not an ordinary case. This is made ex parte, which means that a law officer of the Crown or a police officer goes before a
July 14, 1977

judge with an affidavit and nobody has the right to crossexamine him, and he swears that this and that is the fact. So the judge signs the order on a busy afternoon, and the wiretap is allowed.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Elaving heard only one side of the story.

subtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1977 AMENDMENTS TO CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Yes, and that side has not even been examined by scrutiny of the right of cross-examination. I cannot accept that, and neither can any other lawyer in this country. The law societies of the provinces, the Canadian bar, the Advocates' Society of Ontario, and the benchers of Upper Canada say that this cannot go on, not because lawyers should have any special protection, but because the citizens of Canada have civil rights, and they are entitled to privacy. Have we reached the stage where we can press a red, blue, pink or green button and out rolls our whole lives? What human being is without some sin? What human being does not have some little skeleton in his closet which he would rather keep locked up during his lifetime? What family in this country has not had difficulties? We as members of parliament are not immune because we are in public life. It does not matter which party we belong to; it always saddens me that our lives and the lives of our children and our wives are bared. When this bill goes through, everybody will be subject to that scrutiny, and that is not good enough.

Mr. Speaker, may I just say a few words. I know that both the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) and the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) have condensed their remarks, but I should like to make a few comments because of what has been said, although this question was extensively covered in the minutes of the proceedings of the committee.
May I give the background to this whole situation? The amendments to the Criminal Code in 1974, which provided the legislative regime for electronic surveillance, dealt with the question of privileged communications in only one respect, namely, that tapes of privileged communications could not be introduced in evidence.
The law at that time did not make provision for the actual surveillance of privileged communications. It did not provide any regime other than the normal regime for that situation. As a result of some rather unpleasant incidents, one in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, where the barristers' telephone in the courthouse was bugged, and another in Manitoba involving the wiretapping of judges-both authorizations, I want to make clear, which were authorized in the normal way by judges- concern was expressed by many, including myself, that the law relating to electronic surveillance of lawyers should be changed.
The solicitor general and 1 immediately reviewed the guidelines which are published for the RCMP and for Crown agents setting out a regime by which they would not apply for authorizations against lawyers except in very special circumstances. Several other attorneys general in the provinces did the same thing. But because we were dealing at the time with the wiretap amendments in this bill, I said that this was an opportunity to provide some amendments relating to electronic surveillance of lawyers' telephones.
Obviously the question arises whether there should be some blanket exemption or whether there should be some special rule. I opted, as did the justice and legal affairs committee, for special rules relating to those communications.
I want to emphasize that there are on the committee, members on this side of the House who are knowledgeable on the question of wiretap. I point particularly to the chairman of the justice and legal affairs committee, who unfortunately is out of Canada on parliamentary business, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), who was an active member of the previous parliamentary committee and has been active obviously in this committee. His credentials as a protector of human rights are, I think, unchallenged in this House. Also the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) was very active and concerned on the question of
July 14, 1977

wiretap. Ele examined every word of these amendments very carefully, both with me and my officials.
In working out the amendments I met, in the course of discussion of this whole bill, with a group consisting of the criminal justice chairman of the Canadian Bar Association, with Mr. Borovoy of the Canadian Liberties Association, and with Arthur Whaley, president of the Criminal Lawyers Association of Toronto. In their brief they were very critical of some aspects of the wiretap amendments, and I should like to read to the House what they said:
Apart from the welcome restrictions on the bugging of places ordinarily used by solicitors, nowhere do these amendments even confront the dragnet impact of electronic surveillance. On the contrary, the government bill would increase even further the ambit of permissible surveillance and decrease even further the safeguards for personal privacy.
That was said before further amendments were made to the bill. They went on to say:
Unfortunately, the new restriction on the bugging of places used by solicitors could not even copeand so on. They went on to say:
Even if all of these government amendments had been in force at that time, there would have been nothing to prevent the eavesdropping which took place on the conversations of all the other lawyers and their clients. At a minimum, in our view, the law should be further amended so as to prohibit the interception of privileged communications beyond those which a court has expressly authorized.
I examined those people and Mr. Borovoy made it very clear to me, speaking I take it on behalf of the Canadian Liberties Association, that it would be improper to give a blanket exemption against wiretapping to the legal profession and that they were opposed to it. The position that the civil liberties general counsel took was that we had to put into legislation a special regime to safeguard lawyers' communications and privileged communications on the basis, obviously, that the administration of justice requires that the citizen have an unfettered access and right to advice and counsel by a lawyer. That is precisely what is being done in this bill, and was precisely what was done in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs where further amendments were made.

People want the most freedom that is available to them. I can understand the desire for unlimited freedom, but on the other hand most people also want society to have a sense of security. Most people want a police force that has adequate

means at its disposal to deal with crime. Most people want both things, and the dilemma for people who are framing our laws, or for legislators responsible for laws, is to find some kind of balance between unlimited freedom and the need for security. Society walks that constant tightrope of choice.
What bothers me about much of what goes on in the debates or interventions 1 have heard on this subject, is the refusal to recognize that you cannot have both conditions. You cannot have the unlimited freedom that all of us would desire, you cannot do away with wiretapping, you cannot do away with policemen, you cannot do away with surveillance, and still have the security you want. The question is: what kind of balance do you strike, and do you strike that balance fairly?
I think up until recently our society has tended to go in the direction of absolute freedom. To a very large extent we have been a civil libertarian society; virtually every piece of legislation introduced has increased the protection of the individual and has tried to diminish the role of the police officer.
I think the time has come when society says that precious as those absolute freedoms are, the need for security in our society is also important, and in fact the police have been hamstrung. We have gone too far in terms of preventing the police from doing their job. This is what needs to be faced openly. Just look at the dilemma; you cannot have both things at the same time. It is easy enough to say we are all for the police, we are all for security, we are all for civil liberties. We must make this decision. Trade-offs, never pleasant, popular or easy to make, must be made. Members must be honest with themselves and say what they are doing. I shall try to do this.
I admit that once I was much more fearful of authorities than I am today, much more apprehensive of the police and of the kinds of institutions which existed when I was born, than I am today. I have worked hard all my life to restrict some of the unlimited power those institutions wielded. Those powers needed restricting. The concern for civil liberties was not strong in our society. I take a moment to pay tribute to those who fought for civil liberties, and fought for some of the changes which have come about in our society. But like everything else in society, the pendulum never comes to rest in the middle. It swings too much one way or the other, and must be brought back to the middle, as it were. And that is the dilemma, or crisis if you like, which faces law makers. That is the dilemma which faces people like me who, at one time, may have been considered radicals, who were against authority, who tried to curtail the power of authority. But there comes a time when you ask if our authorities have enough power to do the job they are supposed to do, in order to deal with our society's problems. Frankly, I do not think they have, and they ought to have such power.

The proposal to permit wiretapping with the permission of judges does not meet the needs of this country. We do not have a democratic society in which we have gone too far in the direction of giving people civil liberties. Democracy requires giving people the fullest possible rights and protections.
To my knowledge there is not a member in this House who has followed the counsel given in the United States by very competent and highly respected organizations such as the American Civil Liberties Union, which is opposed to all wiretapping. That is not the case here in this parliament. Not a single member has advocated the complete abolition of wiretapping.
Those of us who support this amendment are not opposing the police any more than did members on both sides of the House who ignored the advice of the police when they voted for the abolition of capital punishment. All those members who voted for the abolition of capital punishment were singularly unimpressed by the arguments of the police in favour of retaining capital punishment. Just as I was prepared to listen and reject the advice of the police on capital punishment, 1 have listened to the advice of the police on this question, and to the advice of others, and I have come to the conclusion we need to restrict much more the rights of the police to engage in wiretapping. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the amendments introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) dealing with Bill C-51.
First, I would like to make it clear that we have always been in favour of law and order-there is no doubt about that. We back perhaps 100 per cent the police departments to maintain law and order in Canada, and we are also in favour of establishing courts of justice and for security. On the other hand, when we examine the history of all those countries where with the same arguments that are being made, namely in the name of security, they want to put up wiretaps and make them available to all police departments in Canada, we fully realize that this gives opposite results.
Mr. Speaker, police reforms are currently under way in Quebec. Everybody knows that municipalities and cities today have lost, not control over police departments but the sense of democracy in that they can no longer from a practical point of view fire those policemen who no longer meet the needs of those municipalities. There are hundreds of cases in Quebec where city councils wanted to fire policemen. Those problems have been before our courts for several years and are not over yet. I could give striking examples, Mr. Speaker.
Furthermore, there is talk at present of taking away from Quebec municipalities the authority they now have over police departments to transfer that authority to the government of Quebec. In that way, the police departments in our municipalities and cities will become with respect to discipline and for all other areas responsible to the government of Quebec. That means that the further away we move authority from the people, the less security we have. This legislation will only trouble ordinary people because criminals, bandits, those who may fear bugging are smart enough not to use the telephone to consult their lawyers. On the other hand, 99.9 per cent of the people-honest people-will have to fear consulting their lawyer because they will not know if his office is not bugged when it is the bandits who should be under surveillance.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation will only bother people as a whole, but it will not solve anything as far as crime is concerned because those who will be directly concerned by this legislation will be smart enough to find ways to elude wiretapping of any police force. Mr. Speaker, municipalities in the province of Quebec-because it will be an ever more critical issue in that province-will have less and less power over police forces and authority will be more and more in the hands of the state. It is also established that the more we rely on the state for our security, the less the ordinary citizen is protected.
For all these reasons and many others, particularly because this legislation will do nothing but annoy honest people in the province of Quebec as well as in other provinces, without changing anything in the crime situation in Canada, I have an obligation to vote for the motion, not out of fanaticism for civil rights, but for liberty alone. I will have an obligation to vote for the amendments of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams).

The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), when speaking about five minutes ago, said have faith in our judges, have faith in our police. -to the judge who granted the authorization that the investigation is continuing and the judge is of the opinion that the interests of justice require that a delay of a determinate reasonable length be granted, in which case the judge may grant a determinate reasonable delay."
I do not know whether the House is in the mood to listen to something that is as mundane as the law we are attempting to amend. I know that is a bit mind-bending for a lot of people here tonight. What we are trying to do with the amendment the Minister of Justice has presented to this House is to take away the discretion of the courts and say that the notification period shall be up to three years.
I would rather trust the judges of this land, and that is what the hon. member for Calgary-North (Mr. Woolliams) is attempting to do with the amendment we have before us. There is no reason in the world to change the law as it stands. It has worked well. It gives the courts a review process that is absolutely vital and necessary in terms of wiretapping. The trouble with this debate is that it gets so simplistic no one looks at what we are trying to change.
I have great respect for the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge. I have respect for his intelligence and intellect. He is an extremely astute member. However, what he has failed to perceive is that liberty is a very delicate flower. The species has developed liberty in a unique and unusual way. Somebody has to defend liberty once in a while because the trends are all against liberty.

We have now considered the wiretap provision and are on questions of parole, which form a very significant part of this legislation.
1 am surprised there was not more interest on the part of parliamentarians about the subject of the penitentiary system. I might say that I appreciate the fact that an all-party committee has reported on the question of penitentiaries in this country. It is an important report. I am glad to see the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) here tonight listening to the debate with some interest.
With regard to the amendments before us under Bill C-51, only one of them relates in any way to the recommendations made by the all-party committee on changes in the penitentiary system, and I am disappointed that at this point we have not yet seen more action.
Perhaps, first of all, I could deal with motions Nos. 35 and 36. Motion No. 35 simply asks that the Parole Board act in accordance with the principles of natural justice in making its determination. I have left the motion general because the principles of natural justice are easily defined by the courts. It is again an attempt to allow the courts an opportunity to exercise their discretion. It is an opportunity to allow the judges to take a look at the parole provisions and ensure that the Parole Board is acting in a fair way. I am not suggesting that we superimpose a whole new set of jurisprudence on the Parole Board. I am only suggesting, in view of the disruption that we have seen in our prison systems, that the Parole Board act in accordance with the principles of natural justice so that there can be more peace and calm within the prison system.
I am not suggesting that the Parole Board should be any more lenient than it is. My argument is that it should have been stronger in some cases. The board leans in the other direction. That does not mean it should not also act in accordance with the rules of natural justice. So, quite simply, motions Nos. 35 and 36 ask that the general principle of the rules of natural justice apply to the operations of the Parole Board.

Mr. Speaker, may I say briefly that, as 1 see it, motion No. 36 requires the board to conduct hearings when it has decided to grant, deny or revoke parole. Motion No. 35 is consequential since it would delete the power of the governor in council to make regulations, prescribing when a hearing must be held, the information to be furnished prior to the hearing, the entitlement to assistance at the hearing, and the occasions on which reasons for decisions would have to be given by the board.
It is a matter of principle on the question of the hearing, and there is no dispute. The question is whether it should be in the regulations or in the statute. 1 believe it is in the interest of the inmates that it be left in the regulations. If we put it into the statute, because of the high number of people who would be involved-I only have to mention, for instance, the number of day parole hearings that would have to be held, or to mention the number of people on short sentences in penitentiaries and provincial prisons where hearings would have to be held to conclude that if we put it into the statute, we would be delaying the procedural safeguards which the board is now maintaining and which it should continue to maintain. That deals with motions Nos. 35 and 36.
With regard to Motion No. 37, the amendment would add a subsection on the procedure to be followed on suspension of parole and subsequent review. The subsection would make it mandatory for the board to hold a hearing as to whether parole would be revoked, unless the board, within 30 days from the date it had the matter referred to it, chooses to cancel the suspension.
This motion is along the same lines as motion No. 36 in that it attempts to incorporate into the legislation a right that the board contemplates will be dealt with under the regulations. The board will be recommending to the governor in council, and so will I shortly, regulations that will require a hearing to be commenced within 30 days following a reference to the board by the person effecting the suspension. I believe once again that this is another occasion where the only difference between what is proposed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and what we will be proposing is the method by which the inmate is to be given certain rights. 1 believe it will be easier to proceed faster in this regard by keeping in the hands of the governor in council the power to make regulations in this regard and to make progress as soon as possible. I understand, however, that the hon. member will be speaking on motion No. 38.

Motion No. 37, to which the Solicitor General referred, deals with the problem inherent in the revocation of parole under the existing law. The revocation of parole, when made, would now be subsequently referred for review by the Parole Board. However, no time limit is provided for the Parole Board in terms of reporting, and my amendment would require that the board report within 30 days so that the inmate would at least have some hope of knowing what decision there would be in the long run. It seems to me that that is a matter which would encourage peace within institutions. The board would have some responsibility not to delay its reports indefinitely. The minister's legislation does not provide for any time limit with regard to that, and I think that that is really a matter of cleaning up the legislation. Perhaps the minister will accept that amendment, which is fairly reasonable.
With regard to motion No. 38, in the past a parolee who violated his parole, subsequently had the time spent on parole added to his sentence. The result could be that a person serving a two year sentence could ultimately spend three or four years in jail because of his violations. Appropriately, the government has attempted to solve that problem by proposing that the time spent on parole not be added to sentences. The difficulty is that the government has failed to include those people who presently are serving time on parole. It seems reasonable to me that they should not be discriminated against by the passage of this legislation, which would apply only to persons being paroled subsequent to the passage of the legislation.
I am asking the Solicitor General to apply the worth-while rule which he has brought into the legislation to parolees who are now on parole. This would not affect those whose parole was previously violated and revoked and who have been recommitted to prison. I am asking the Solicitor General not to discriminate between those who are now properly on parole and not violating their parole and those who may subsequently be paroled. It seems to me that it would be a fairly logical step for the Solicitor General not to discriminate between those two classes.
1 support the amendment, but we are discriminating against those who are presently on parole. We are allowing the legislation to apply only to those who are subsequently paroled.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED DIFFERENTIATION IN TREATMENT BY CUSTOMS BETWEEN FORCES PERSONNEL AND CIVILIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what brings us together is my question of the other day to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) about the practices of the Armed Forces in dealing with people moving through customs, namely, National Defence people, and about whether they should have to make a declaration if it is felt they had made purchases abroad of $50 or less. The practice for the population as a whole is that they do not have to make any declaration or they may make an oral declaration, and they do not have to fill in any forms. In maritime command personnel do have to fill in a form. Having looked at the documents I can say that somebody in the department has misinterpreted the practice in general, and maritime command people have been required to fill in the form, whereas the rest of the personnel can move back and forth and be treated as civilians.
I am somewhat hampered in this debate because 1 have probably mislaid the document I once had. I have looked for it in my office and here in my desk. I cannot find it. In any event, a directive was sent out by maritime command stating that these forms did have to be filled in, but the rest of National Defence was not required to do so. I think there is a misunderstanding, and when I raised this matter the other day the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of National Defence thought one thing, but when I showed the Minister of National Defence the documents, he indicated to me that probably in one part of National Defence there had been a mistake, and that was going to be corrected. 1 have probably taken more of the time of the House than i originally intended.
I think the parliamentary secretary will straighten this up, and I thank the House for its indulgence.

July 14, 1977

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice A. Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED DIFFERENTIATION IN TREATMENT BY CUSTOMS BETWEEN FORCES PERSONNEL AND CIVILIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's brevity, considering the fact that it is past ten o'clock. Perhaps we could ask search and rescue to find his document for him, but in this case I have the answer to his question, and I think it will alleviate his justified concern.
Canadian Forces administrative orders state that goods valued at $50 and under may be declared verbally unless a customs official requests a written declaration.
Apparently in the past customs officials have been requesting written declarations from service personnel, but as a result of an interdepartmental inquiry the Department of National Revenue has agreed to process service personnel in the same manner as civilians.
The message referred to by the hon. member was issued from maritime command headquarters on June 23, 1977, and contravenes the Canadian Forces administrative order in so far that it "directs a requirement for written declarations" without qualification that goods valued at $50 or less may be declared orally except when directed otherwise by a customs official.
Maritime command has been directed to clarify the instruction and to ensure that the procedures outlined in the Canadian Forces administrative order issued by National Defence headquarters are adhered to. Maritime command will change the message and will adhere to the Canadian Forces administrative order.
